notes.meaning: Most old Christian writers read this song as a picture of the love between Christ and his people. Matthew Henry and Wesley hear the groom, Christ, speaking here. He calls himself a lovely, sweet-smelling flower that grows in the open field, where anyone may come and enjoy him. Other commentators hear the bride speaking humbly, calling herself just a simple wildflower, perhaps a crocus-like meadow flower rather than a rose.

The groom answers that his love stands out among other women like a lily among thorn bushes. Christ treasures his church, meaning all his people, above everything else. The thorns stand for the wicked world, which can scratch and hurt believers. Even so, believers must stay lilies and not turn into thorns. One day they will be moved to a garden with no thorns at all.

The bride replies that her beloved stands out like a fruit tree in a wild forest. The world is like a barren tree, but Christ is fruitful. His shade means rest and protection for people worn out by guilt or trouble. His fruit means his sweet gifts, such as forgiveness, peace and his promises. It is not enough to walk past this shade; we must sit down under it.

The "house of wine" is a banquet hall where the king feasts with his friends. Spiritually, Christ brings believers into close friendship with him. Commentators link this to worship and the Lord's Supper, the meal of bread and cup Christians share. A banner is a flag. His flag over her says "love": he won her by love and keeps her safe under it.

She is so overcome by love that she feels weak and asks for raisin cakes and apples to strengthen her. She is overwhelmed by joy, not by sorrow. Spiritually, she longs for more of Christ's comfort, not less. Some Christians have felt God's love so strongly that they could hardly bear more.

Here is a tender picture: his left hand holds up her head, and his right arm hugs her. Christ holds up his weak and weary people. He gives them sure proof of his love. No one can pull them out of his hands.

She solemnly asks the women of Jerusalem not to disturb love. Gazelles and deer are shy animals, easily startled, so love must be treated gently. Spiritually, believers should take care not to break their closeness with Christ by sin, or to grieve the Holy Spirit. The Geneva Notes read it as a charge not to trouble the peace of the church.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read this as a warning not to stir up romantic love in yourself before its right time, when God awakens it.

notes.meaning: She hears his voice and sees him bounding over the hills like a deer. Christ comes gladly and quickly, and no mountain of difficulty can stop him. Matthew Henry applies this to Old Testament believers looking ahead to Christ coming as a man. The Geneva Notes say Christ took on our human nature to help his church. Even when he seems far away, he soon returns.

He stands outside the wall and looks in through the windows and lattice. Old Testament believers caught glimpses of Christ through sacrifices and ceremonies. We too see him only in part for now, through his Word and the sacraments (baptism and the Lord's Supper). One day we will see him face to face. Matthew Henry adds that the wall can be our own sin, and Christ waits behind it, ready to forgive.

He calls her his darling and his beautiful one, and invites her to get up and come with him. Whatever others think of her, to him she is lovely. Christ invites people to leave sin and empty things behind and come close to him. His warm words reassure her that he still loves her.

Spring has come. The cold rains are gone, flowers bloom, birds sing, figs ripen and vines smell sweet. Christ's coming drives back sin and error, like spring after winter. It also pictures a person coming to faith, comfort after a sad season, and the hope of rising from the dead. Even small first signs of holy living please God. He repeats "Arise, come away" because he truly longs for her.

He calls her his dove, hiding in the cracks of a rocky cliff. Christ is the Rock where his people are safe. She may be hiding out of fear or shame over her sin. He gently calls her to show her face and speak to him boldly in prayer. Her voice is sweet to him and her face is lovely.

Little foxes can ruin vineyards just when the vines are in bloom. Spiritually, these are small sins and the first stirrings of wrong desires, which can spoil new growth in faith. They can also stand for false teaching that harms the church. Whatever hinders us from good must be removed.

She rejoices: "My beloved is mine and I am his." Believers have Christ as their own, with all his gifts. They also belong to him, because he made them and bought them back. Feeding among the lilies shows that Christ loves to be present among his people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: In Catholic devotion, Mary is honored as the "mystical rose" and often pictured with a lily, as the lily without equal among God's holy people.

notes.meaning: She asks her beloved to come swiftly like a deer over rugged mountains. "Bether" probably means mountains that divide. The breaking day may picture the dawn of the gospel, when the shadows of Old Testament ceremonies passed away. It may also picture Christ's return, when all our darkness ends. Until then, she prays that he will come over every barrier and comfort her.
